extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) involved in U.S. patent examination and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 2014 Interim USPTO subject matter eligibility (35 U.S.C. § 101) analysis during examination, including the Alice/Mayo two-part test, product-of-nature (markedly different) analysis, and required form-paragraph rejections. Intended to be used when evaluating whether claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determines whether the claim is directed to a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. This step has not changed and is explained in MPEP 2106(I). If the claim is not directed to one of these statutory categories, reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being drawn to non-statutory subject matter, using revised form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01, and continue examination for patentability. If the claim is directed to a statutory category, proceed to Step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP 2106(I) for details. Apply form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 when rejecting for non-statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — two-part Alice/Mayo analysis (Steps 2A and 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part analysis from Alice Corp. (also called the Mayo test) for claims directed to laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas (the judicially recognized exceptions). This analysis is to be used during examination for evaluating whether a claim is drawn to patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2 is represented in diamonds (2A) and (2B) of the flowchart and is the subject of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — determine whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicial exceptions). If no, the claim is eligible and examination should continue for patentability. If yes, proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of the types of concepts that the courts have found to be laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas are provided in Parts I.A.2 and IV of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'directed to'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Directed to" means the exception is recited in the claim, i.e., the claim sets forth or describes the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Part I.A.1 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance for how to identify when an exception is 'recited' in the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when claim does not 'tie up' an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim when viewed as a whole clearly does not seek to 'tie up' any judicial exception, use the 'streamlined analysis' discussed in Part I.B.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The streamlined analysis is an alternative path under Step 2A when the claim clearly does not risk preempting the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim recites a nature-based product limitation, the markedly different characteristics analysis is used to evaluate whether the claim is directed to a 'product of nature' that falls under the law of nature and natural phenomenon exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To determine whether the markedly different characteristics analysis is needed, and how to perform this analysis, see Part I.A.3 of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — 'significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether any element, or combination of elements, in the claim is sufficient to ensure that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception. If no, the claim is ineligible and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 101 using form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. If yes, the claim is eligible. In either case, examination should continue for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider additional elements both individually and as an ordered combination. Use the Supreme Court considerations and examples in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance to evaluate 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider additional elements individually and as an ordered combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The additional elements should be considered both individually and as an ordered combination. Individual elements when viewed on their own may not appear to add significantly more, but when viewed in combination may amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether elements that appear generic alone produce a meaningful limitation when combined in the claimed ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court considerations for determining 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has identified a number of considerations for determining whether a claim with additional elements amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of these considerations, and how they are applied, are provided in Parts I.B.1 and III of the Interim Eligibility Guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider each claim separately based on the particular elements recited therein – claims do not automatically rise or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a determination for one claim applies to other claims even if similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim recites multiple exceptions, analyze one exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is directed to a plurality of exceptions, conduct the eligibility analysis for one of the exceptions. Additional elements that satisfy Step 2B for one exception will likely satisfy Step 2B for all exceptions in a claim. On the other hand, if the claim fails under Step 2B for one exception, the claim is ineligible, and no further eligibility analysis is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an exception and apply Steps 2A/2B; a failure on one chosen exception is sufficient to deem the claim ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05 — Rejection heading and examiner usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Form Paragraph 7.05: 'Claim [1] rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because' (Heading only) — used to begin a §101 rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph must be preceded by form paragraph 7.04.01 in first actions and final rejections. (2) This form paragraph must be followed by a detailed explanation of the grounds of rejection using one or more of form paragraphs - 7.05.01, 7.05.015, 7.05.02, 7.05.03, or another appropriate reason. (3) See MPEP §§ 706.03(a) and 2105 - 2107.03 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05.01 — Rejection for non-statutory (not one of four categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'the claimed invention is directed to non-statutory subject matter. The claim(s) does not fall within at least one of the four categories of patent eligible subject matter because [1]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note: (1) This form paragraph should be preceded by form paragraph 7.05. (2) In bracket 1, explain why the claimed invention is not patent eligible subject matter by identifying what the claim(s) is/are directed to and explain why it does not fall within at least one of the four categories recited in 35 U.S.C. 101 (process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter), e.g., the claim(s) is/are directed to a signal per se, mere information in the form of data, a contract between two parties, or a human being (see MPEP § 2106, subsection I). (3) For a claim that is directed to a judicial exception and is non-statutory, use form paragraph 7.05.015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraph 7.05.015 — Rejection for judicial exception without significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Template: 'the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception (i.e., a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea) without significantly more. Claim(s) [1] is/are directed to [2]. The claim(s) does/do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception because [3].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner Note guidance: (1) Precede with form paragraph 7.05. (2) For all claim types and any judicial exception. (3) In bracket 1, identify the claim(s) that recite the judicial exception. (4) In bracket 2, identify the exception by referring to how it is recited in the claim and explain why it is considered an exception (examples: 'the Arrhenius equation, which is a law of nature in the form of a mathematical algorithm' or 'the series of steps instructing how to hedge risk, which is a fundamental economic practice and thus an abstract idea'). For products of nature, explain how the characteristics are not markedly different from the naturally occurring counterpart (example: 'the naturally occurring DNA segment, which is not markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart because it conveys the same genetic information'). Provide additional explanation when appropriate. (5) In bracket 3, identify the additional elements and explain why, when considered separately and in combination, they do not add significantly more — e.g., generically recited computer elements are routine in any computer implementation and do not add a meaningful limitation; steps for routine data gathering to test a correlation do not add a meaningful limitation.
